title: Editorial summary and tone
prompt: City centers should reduce private car traffic, not because cars are inherently harmful, but because current street design prioritizes speed over public life. Supporters of the change argue that quieter streets improve health, increase local commerce, and make commuting more predictable. Critics worry that delivery times and commuter flexibility will suffer during the transition.
instructions: Read the passage and write a short summary that states the main idea, one supporting point, and the writer's tone.
supportNote: Aim for 3 to 4 sentences and mention both the argument and the tone.
sampleAnswer: The passage argues that city centers should reduce private car traffic because current streets favor speed over community life. It supports this by linking calmer streets to health and local business benefits, while acknowledging concerns about deliveries and commuter flexibility. The tone is balanced but clearly supportive of reform.

title: Opinion paragraph upgrade
prompt: Should universities require all students to take a communication course, even if it is outside their major?
instructions: Write one clear paragraph in response to the prompt. Use at least one connector and one reasoned example.
supportNote: Keep the paragraph focused: position, reason, and example.
sampleAnswer: Universities should require a communication course because most professions now depend on clear writing and speaking, not only technical knowledge. For example, engineers and designers often need to explain complex ideas to clients or multidisciplinary teams. Therefore, a communication course would strengthen employability and improve collaboration across fields.

title: Listening detail capture
prompt: Listen to the short debate and summarize the speaker's final position and one contrasting detail.
instructions: Write a short summary of the speaker's conclusion and one contrast they mention.
listeningPromptText: Okay, so we've talked a lot about remote work, and honestly, it's fantastic for many people. It's convenient, saves time, and can boost productivity. However, I think we need to be realistic about junior team members. They really benefit from being in the office, even just a few times a week. It's about more than formal training, you know? It's the quick questions, the observing, the informal feedback. That's harder to replicate remotely. So, a hybrid approach feels best - balancing convenience with crucial early career development.
supportNote: Playback now prefers the bundled sample audio asset and falls back to prompt playback when no file is available.
sampleAnswer: The speaker ends up supporting a hybrid model, arguing that junior employees need regular in-person mentoring even if remote work is convenient. The contrast is that convenience matters, but training and informal feedback matter more early in a career.

title: Spoken argument and retry
prompt: Do you agree that remote work is harder for junior employees than for experienced employees? Explain your position.
instructions: Answer the prompt aloud. For the MVP, use transcript capture or load the guided transcript sample, then submit for feedback.
starterText: I partly agree because junior employees usually need faster feedback and more structure. However, remote work can still work if teams create regular mentoring routines and clear communication habits.
supportNote: Speaking v1 uses transcript-first practice before deeper pronunciation scoring.
sampleAnswer: I agree that remote work is usually harder for junior employees because they need quick feedback, observation, and informal learning opportunities that are easier to access in person. However, this does not mean remote work is impossible. If teams offer structured mentoring, regular check-ins, and clear expectations, junior staff can still develop effectively.
